articles.title: The GOP’s Enemy #1 for the Midterms: Socialism
articles.author: Ben Burgis
articles.content: A very old joke imagines two elderly Jewish men sitting on a park bench. The first reads the local Yiddish-language newspaper. The second reads an antisemitic, pro-fascist paper. After a few minutes, the first turns to the second and asks, “How can you read that garbage?” The second replies, “When I read your paper, it’s nothing but bad news. It depresses me! When I read this paper, I hear that we run banks, the media, Hollywood. . . . It cheers me up!” I kept thinking of that yesterday as I watched the first night of the Republicans’ midterm “ convention ” (where no one was nominated, and no official business of any kind was conducted). When I read Jacobin , I get a (sadly realistic) view of reality where the Democratic establishment remains powerful and opposed to even basic reforms like Medicare for All. When I listened to the “convention” speakers, on the other hand, I heard that socialists had completely taken over the Democratic ballot line. Congressman Steve Scalise said there had been a “Bolshevik Revolution in the Democrat party.” In fact, the socialist takeover seemed to be one of the few subjects most of the speakers could get excited about. Two years ago, the (actual) Republican convention that nominated Donald Trump was magnetically disturbing, like something out of a darkly satirical movie about a country descending into dystopian authoritarianism. Hulk Hogan ripped off his shirt while screaming about “Trumpomania.” Speaker after speaker spun unhinged horror stories about hordes of undocumented immigrants poisoning the native-born populace. The energy was palpable. Now, Trump has been back in office for a year and a half. In that time, we’ve seen continuing inflation, a wildly unpopular war in the Middle East, something like a Cold War against Canada of all countries, and an immigration crackdown that has been cruel and authoritarian enough to turn the public decisively against the administration on what was once their most popular issue. Even in the context of a glorified pep rally full of attendees prepared to cheer anything that comes out of any low-level Republican politician’s mouth, convention speakers palpably struggled to find a narrative and stoke excitement about it. Where once the idea of restoring Trump to the presidency and making their enemies pay was enough to whip Republicans into a frenzy, now, as often as not, congressmen addressing the crowd seemed happy to wander listlessly from issue to issue. The palpable exception was the struggle against the scourge of socialism. On that , they sounded like their old selves. Heavy on Red-Baiting, Light on Specifics House Majority Whip Tom Emmer railed against “the Communist Party, uh, excuse me, the Democrats,” the “democratic communists” — presumably his way of referring to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) — and the “Marxists, communists, and anarchists” who he said want to “destroy” America. Not to be outdone, Trump himself said in his keynote that: In state after state, the Democrat establishment has been overthrown and replaced by crazed lunatics and radicals. They call themselves Democrat socialists, but actually they’re communists. . . . It’s going to be a communist country if they win. What, though, would being a “communist country” actually entail? How would the laws change? How would society change? On that, the “convention” speakers were far less informative. There was a lot of talk of “taxes” going up, but they made little to no mention of which taxes would be raised on which taxpayers, never mind what would be paid for in exchange. Scalise, Emmer, and Trump all trotted out the DSA platform’s dubious slogan (controversial within DSA itself) about a long-term goal of “abolishing” police and prisons. But none of them mentioned short-term goals on which DSA is completely united, like Medicare for All (a phrase none of them uttered even once) or universal daycare or abolishing the travesties of Americans going into debt to pay for medical bills or a college education. Emmer mentioned “health care for illegals” while managing to avoid the subject of whether the 96.7 percent of the people who live here who aren’t undocumented immigrants would also get free health care. Perhaps the most fervent bigots are so incensed about the thought of that 3.3 percent of “illegals” getting to see a doctor when they’re sick without having to worry about medical bankruptcy that they think having to worry about medical bankruptcy themselves is a fair trade. But even among Republican-leaning voters, that’s likely a minority position — and politicians like Emmer know it, which is why they aren’t eager to broach the subject. Similarly, he said something about “Mamdani the commie” wanting to build what he said would be substandard municipal housing, but he couldn’t bring himself to mention the mayor’s rent freeze or his hearings to expose and go after negligent landlords. Perhaps bringing up those subjects would have encouraged otherwise sympathetic working-class Republicans to think a little too hard about how much they themselves pay in rent, and what their complaints are about their own landlords. All in all, in this threatening scenario, electing politicians like “Mamdani the commie” might not sound like the worst idea. Even the long-term agenda of full socialism is one Republican red-baiters don’t want to linger on for too long. It’s one thing to say in an applause line that America will never become a “communist country.” It’s another to look into democratic socialists’ ideas about what a fully socialist society might actually look like . Imagine if, instead of just saying that socialists want to “defund the police and abolish prisons and get rid of the Senate,” they had to try to whip up their base about the core socialist economic agenda. Perhaps Trump could have said something like this: These crazed radical-left lunatics don’t just want to give everyone health care, so that you’d no more have to take out your credit card at the hospital than you do when the fire department comes to put out a fire at your house, but they even want to make public daycare available to anyone who wants it. And you know what they want to do long term? You’re not going to believe this! They’re going to take away our beloved corporations from rich people like me and turn them over to the workers to run themselves. The people who worked there would hold elections about who ran the company. They would get to vote on the wage scales, to decide how much everyone would be paid! Can you imagine? The workers? That would be ridiculous! Trump knows better than to give that speech. It’s so much safer, from his perspective, to stick to cherry-picked, internally controversial bits and pieces of the DSA platform. Unfortunately for him, though, the public is already aware of at least some elements of democratic socialists’ core economic agenda. And in the long term, banking on ordinary people to hate immigrants more than they want health care or lower rent may be a losing proposition.

articles.title: Found, But Not Rescued
articles.content: In the middle of the ocean, a man was drowning. He could not hold fast to the ropes dangling from the bow and stern of the bulk carrier that stopped to help. Below, a small, blue wooden boat crammed with people was tossed by a raging storm. As high winds sloshed water over the deck, the passengers — who had sailed for a day and a night without drinking water — rushed toward the swaying ropes. But the lines slipped through their hands. The children lacked the strength to climb. Even for the strong, a single slip could mean being crushed beneath the swaying hull of the massive ship. “ We were all very scared in the moment and drove away from [the] big ship,” Daniel, a survivor from Eritrea, reportedly told rescuers, describing how the migrant boat he was on powered away from the larger vessel in fear of being capsized. (Daniel is a pseudonym because survivors of deadly rescues at sea often face criminalization.) “ We tried to help, to throw [life rings],” to the man in the water, Daniel continued, ​ “ but he didn’t take it. We saw him go far away and we knew he [was] dying.” When people drown, they don’t scream or wave; they fall silently. Their mouths gasp at the surface, and their arms and legs move like they’re climbing a ladder underwater — until they simply disappear. As the night’s darkness enveloped the 81 migrants remaining on the wooden boat, the man in the water slipped out of sight. With no means of navigation, those left on board could only follow the flare of oil platforms as raw markers of north — or look to the stars to guide them. The migrants’ voyage, which had begun four nights earlier, on May 20 , 2025 , was described to me in great detail by rescue crewmembers who gathered Daniel’s testimony, along with that of others aboard the blue wooden boat, in the hours after the rescue. The voyage had begun in Libya’s coastal town of Sabratha, where two wooden boats set sail for Italy carrying 245 migrants, according to the rescuers. One of the migrant boats, carrying 128 people, was eventually rescued by the Italian Coast Guard after a civilian alarm system raised an alert. But Daniel’s boat, carrying 117 people, was less fortunate, hitting bad weather near the Sabratha oil platform more than 60 miles off the Libyan coast. What unfolded next — including unfinished rescue attempts by passing merchant vessels, three deaths and the return of 35 migrants to a Libyan detention center known for systemic torture — is the subject of intense legal and moral debate, drawing in multiple governments, international agencies, coast guards, NGOs and commercial shipping companies. At its heart lie serious potential violations of international human rights and refugee law. But the deeper story is structural, rooted in decades of northbound wealth transfer, policies that facilitate unsafe migration routes and systems that drive vulnerable people into the hands of traffickers and abusers. The 2015 launch of Operation Sophia, a European Union military operation designed to ​ “ disrupt human smuggling and trafficking networks,” increased surveillance on the Mediterranean Sea. But deaths at sea never stopped. Regular drones and planes from the European border agency Frontex hum over the waves, but the surveillance is geared at security, not protection. (Frontex disputes this.) Today, Frontex does not perform rescues; instead, it uses a fleet of planes and drones to spot boats in distress. The agency’s crews radio the rescue coordination centers responsible for that stretch of sea, giving them the boats’ position, course and speed and copying neighboring centers on the same call, according to Frontex spokesman Chris Borowski. In situations like Daniel’s, the Libyans may intercept the vessels — if they are in the Libyan search and rescue area — using boats donated by Italy. The migrants are then taken, or returned, to detention centers where survivors report widespread abuses. In August 2025, the Ocean Viking, the rescue boat pictured above, came under heavy machine gun fire, reportedly from Libyan forces sailing a vessel gifted to them by Italy. The attack grounded the ship, stopping all rescues for months. Photo by Ali Arkady In 2025 , nearly 8 , 000 people died or went missing on dangerous migration routes, including those spanning the Mediterranean Sea between Africa and Europe, the Atlantic Ocean from West Africa toward the Canary Islands, and the Horn of Africa toward Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). IOM also found that in the same year , ​ “ 270 human remains washed ashore on Mediterranean coasts,” pointing to untraced shipwrecks. So far in 2026 , at least 990 people have died trying to cross the Mediterranean — far more than the same period last year — including 53 migrants lost at sea in early February, their bodies seemingly washing up on Italy’s beaches following a violent winter storm. Days before that disaster, at least 15 migrants died in Greek waters, reportedly after their boat ​ “ collided ” with a Greek Coast Guard vessel. The man Daniel watched drown last May might never be included in NGO tallies of the dead. But his death still poses a vital question: Why was he — and later two others from the same boat, another man and a child, according to rescuers — allowed to die while trying to reach one of the wealthiest continents on earth? These are not just tragic accidents; they are potential crimes against humanity that could be prosecuted up official chains of command. Now, human rights lawyers are asking the International Criminal Court to investigate European leaders, alongside Libyan suspects, following the death of 25 , 000 asylum seekers and the abuses of 150 , 000 survivors detained in Libya. Of the 117 migrants who set off from Libya on the boat with Daniel, only 79 made it to Italy — feverish, fuel-burned and in shock. But all of them — the survivors, the dead and those returned to Libya — were equally victims, not just of the sea, but of hostile migration policies. These people ​ “ are the ones that we know, who have relatives back in Africa, in the Middle East, who could put the dots together,” said Fellipe Lopes, a bearded Brazilian man then working on board the Ocean Viking , a rescue ship operated by European NGO SOS Mediterranee. With emotion in his voice, Lopes recalled, ​ “ You see a lot of activity [on that sea] — it is such a busy route with vessels, tankers, container vessels, plus military assets in the air and sea, and yet, people continue to drop constantly.” “ There are thousands of people we don’t know about,” Lopes said, ​ “ because they are just missing.” The Ocean Viking was part of a group of around a dozen ships sponsored by civil society groups that work to bring migrants stranded in the Central Mediterranean ashore to Europe, filling the void left by the end of Italian rescue operation ​ “ Mare Nostrum,” or ​ “ Our Sea” — a massive search-and-rescue effort that saved thousands of lives until it was ended , thanks to political and financial pressure, in 2014 . At first, NGO rescue boats hoping to replace the Italian mission worked in concert with European authorities, but their movements later became increasingly restricted after Italy introduced new hard-line, anti-immigration legislation framed as anti-smuggling. (The Italian Coast Guard still performs rescues between Tunisia and the Italian island of Lampedusa, but it does not usually operate farther south towards Libya.) Today, the NGO rescue boats attract a band of mostly European sailors with a punk aesthetic who reject the continent’s far-right, anti-migration turn and want to practice the dying art of humanitarianism. The Ocean Viking is a large, red-and-white offshore tugboat, equipped with radar, a small hospital and living quarters for the crew. I joined the boat to document the crew’s rescue work in May 2025 . We set sail from Syracuse, Sicily, and from there, veered south through a large storm towards Libya, pausing off the coast of Tunisia by the port city of Sfax to rescue 276 shipwrecked migrants. The morning of that rescue, an alert sounded at 3 : 53 a.m. on the ship’s radios. Seafarers pulled on their life vests, boots and waterproof trousers in the storeroom; out on deck, the lifeboats were being lowered down and hit the water by 4 a.m. "Of the 117 migrants who set off from Libya on the boat with Daniel, only 79 made it to Italy—feverish, fuel-burned and in shock. But all of them—the survivors, the dead and those returned to Libya—were equally victims, not just of the sea, but of hostile migration policies." In the dark, fear of the unknown often freezes migrants, one sailor told me, and rescuers rely on this alarm at the sight of an unknown ship to help keep migrant boats at a safe distance. This is the moment when most rescues go wrong, since migrants are often so relieved that they start to celebrate — sometimes jumping up and down, inadvertently causing their ship to capsize. But fear of the unknown can also keep survivors still while translators on the rescue ship explain that they’re sending out smaller boats to meet them. Out on the deck of the Ocean Viking after the rescues, the Mediterranean air was warm and the sea calm. It was black night but there was light from the moon. Below me was the dark sea, swirling like milky blue tea and churning frothy whirlpools against the lifeboats now launching on the port side. Amid the hum of the generators, sloshing of seawater and clomping of rubber boots, there was an atmosphere of sad diligence and worn-down optimism, broken occasionally by levity and games. The drama and intensity of the rescues was punctuated by long hours watching the waves; groups of migrant men passed the time sleeping or smoking. The sailors washed the deck and organized food handouts, tea and hot chocolate stations, and lines for the migrants to wash and charge their phones. One morning, I watched a sailor bent down, absorbed in the task of trying to dry a soaking wet passport with a hair dryer. In the early 1990 s, Spain and Italy introduced visa requirements for North African migrants, closing a period of some fluid movement. Before the Westernled wars in Iraq, Libya and Afghanistan, migration across the Mediterranean was mostly viewed in economic and not criminal terms. This shifted after the 2011 Libyan war, which ​ “ opened the door of Africa to Europe,” said Felippo Aquilino, another rescuer on board the Ocean Viking. Aquilino, a Sicilian with salt-and-pepper hair, had known about the migrant route since a fishing boat full of strangers crashed outside his family’s cabin on the south coast of Lampedusa when he was five years old. He sat talking to me on the deck of the boat under bright sunshine and a strong wind. As an outpost that represents one of the nearest parts of Europe to Africa, Lampedusa has become such a symbol of the deadly Mediterranean crossing that Pope Francis famously made it the destination of his first official trip outside Rome in 2013 , celebrating mass on an altar fashioned from the wood of shipwrecked migrant boats. It’s common for children to be among the migrants saved from boats shipwrecked while crossing the Mediterranean: over half of the 53 people the Ocean Viking rescued from Daniel’s boat in May 2025 were children. (Photos by Ali Arkady) During the second rescue on the morning of May 17 , day broke in full color over the deck as the survivors appeared, clambering up from the lifeboats one by one into the morning and the noise and heat of the engines. And then there on the horizon was another blue wooden boat, listing violently and full of people frozen with fear. The rescuers pulled them into their lifeboats, water moving below their feet as they worked. It’s a strange environment for land people to work in, one of the sailors told me later. The survivors had been sailing for days. They told me stories of trying to reach Europe on crowded boats, only to be captured at sea and sent back by Libyan forces, presumably the EU-equipped Libyan Coast Guard. The day after he was rescued, Ahmed — a Marxist from Sudan who said he fled Darfur in 2019 , when his political activism made him an enemy of both the government and the rebels — told me that, for him, ​ “ There’s no way back, because I refuse two systems, not one.” He tried to cross the sea to reach Europe five times between 2019 and 2025 , but each time, he was returned by Libyan patrol boats. Sometimes, he was sent back and freed along with his fellow travellers. But on other occasions, he said, he was sent to jails where he was tortured. Once, he was forced to pay the equivalent of $ 310 for his freedom. After his release, militias in Misrata forced him to work as a cleaner and guard — sometimes for pay, sometimes not, in a mix of indentured servitude and slavery. Sitting on the deck of the Ocean Viking and looking out at the sea, a metal cross round his neck, another migrant named Josef described leaving Ethiopia’s city of Gondar because he couldn’t find work or money. In Libya, he’d been captured and sent to jail four times: twice for trying to cross the sea and twice just for being on the street. In jail, he said, he’d been kicked ​ “ like an animal” by guards until he could gather the bribe money to escape. Sitting with the women and children outside their sleeping quarters, Helen, a young woman with a mournful air, said she was traveling with her husband. She was tired and withdrawn and didn’t join in when the other women sang and danced on deck with relief. The couple traveled from Ethiopia to Sudan and then Libya, where her husband took menial work. ​ “ Sometimes,” Helen recalled, the militia men ​ “ took him away, kidnapped him, and asked for money to release him.” The first time she tried to cross the sea, Libyans shot at their plastic boat and forced them off. ​ “ The men jumped in the water and the women cried, ​ ‘ Our brothers, please help get them.’” The men were rescued and then beaten by the guards. The second time, she was at sea for 12 hours before being captured and taken back to a prison in Libya, where she was held for nine months. She didn’t have words to describe how bad the treatment was there; when I asked about it, her eyes filled with tears and she began to rock back and forth. From Sfax, we headed to northern Italy, more than 600 miles away, to disembark the survivors under orders from Italian maritime authorities. After four days sailing together, I watched as the migrants stepped down from the boat, many without shoes or socks, to meet a delegation of local officials, the Italian Red Cross and the police. From here, they would start the next part of their journeys. A month later, Ahmed met the photographer I was traveling with, Ali, in Paris. Ahmed had walked all the way to France, crossing the Alps, with the help of kind strangers who treated his worn-out feet and bad stomach. Often, migrants are so relieved to see an NGO rescue boat like the Ocean Viking that they start to celebrate—sometimes jumping up and down, inadvertently causing their small, overcrowded ships to capsize. (Photos by Ali Arkady) In 2013 , after the Arab Spring pro-democracy revolutions and foreign interventions curdled into war, crisis and displacement, Italy responded to the surge in migrant crossings and deaths at sea by launching ​ “ Mare Nostrum.” However, responsibility was later shifted to Frontex, which emphasized border security over rescue, creating a deadly gap in the Central Mediterranean. In a 2025 press release , Frontex boasted of a 20 % drop in ​ “ irregular border crossings” into Europe in the first five months of the year, attributing the decline to thousands of their officers working with national authorities to ​ “ safeguard borders and save lives at sea.” Frontex’s budget surged to 1 . 1 billion euros in 2026 , with an emphasis on funding high-tech surveillance. The agency relies on the Heron 1 drones manufactured by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and contracts with Airbus to provide surveillance drones over the Mediterranean. The agency frames this as a tool for safety, but the nearly 1 billion euros committed to long-term aerial surveillance since 2024 has done little to stop the death toll. Instead, it has facilitated a policy of remote detection and Libyan interception. Frontex spokesman Chris Borowski said in response to inquiries from In These Times: ​ “ Detection is what starts the rescue. In 2025 , Frontex assets contributed to saving 33 , 000 lives, and we’re past 7 , 000 already this year. … On the interception chain and non-refoulment: we comply with non-refoulment in everything we do, full stop.” (Non-refoulement is a core principle under international human rights law prohibiting states from returning a person to a territory where they face real risks of persecution or irreparable harm.) Borowski added: ​ “ When one of our aircraft finds a boat that’s about to sink, the job in that moment is to stop people from drowning. Saving those lives has to come first, because the alternative is watching people drown while everyone works out the politics. What a government does after an interception, Italy, Libya, or anyone else, is a separate and serious question, but it doesn’t change the fact that reporting a boat in distress is what keeps the people on it alive long enough for that question to even come up.” “ I don’t dispute that the reports of torture and extortion in Libyan detention are real and well documented. But the fix for that isn’t asking Frontex to stop reporting boats in distress, a duty every vessel at sea carries,” Borowski said. ​ “ It’s a decision on the political level. That call isn’t ours to make, and we won’t speak as though it is.” A medic on board the Sumud Flotilla that sailed towards Gaza in September 2025 recalled watching Frontex drones with his fellow crewmembers. While the drones only monitor migrant traffic, the sheer number of them was disconcerting, said the medic, speaking on the condition of anonymity. The constant air surveillance ​ “ felt intimidating and dystopian,” he added. Far-right politicians began to denigrate NGO operators as "sea taxis" or accomplices to smugglers, said the Ocean Viking’s Aquilino. This criminalization is a key vector in Europe’s broader hostility to migrants from countries destabilized by corruption, repression, and Western-backed wars and economic policies. In 2017 , the Italian government began introducing rules limiting the operations of NGO ships, followed by new laws carrying penalties in 2019 , and further restrictions during the pandemic. Under mounting pressure from the far Right, Italy enacted the ​ “ Piantedosi Decree ” in 2023 . Named after Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi, the law imposed strict new limitations on NGO rescue operations, requiring vessels to head immediately to the port designated by authorities after every rescue and making ​ “ multi-rescue” missions much harder. That has the effect of reducing the time rescuers can spend at sea answering distress calls, driving up costs and increasing the likelihood of criminalization if paperwork is not filed correctly. Ships are now regularly detained for conducting additional rescues after being assigned a port of disembarkation. Far-right politicians began to denigrate NGO operators as ​ “ sea taxis ” or accomplices to smugglers, said the Ocean Viking’s Aquilino. This criminalization is a key vector in Europe’s broader hostility to migrants from countries destabilized by corruption, repression and Western-backed wars and economic policies. The impact on operations has been huge. Before the war against NGO ships began, Aquilino said, the Ocean Viking spent roughly 300 days a year patrolling for distressed boats; under the Piantedosi Decree, that has dropped to 180 days. It was a sad irony that a year after the EU received the 2012 Nobel Peace Prize for decades of contributions to peace, democracy and human rights worldwide, ​ “ they started closing the borders and stopping the rescues,” he added. After the EU signed a deal with Turkey in 2016 to reduce migration, Ocean Viking crewmember Lopes said there was a sudden increase in the number of Frontex personnel, boats, airplanes, drones and bases around Lesbos, the Greek island off Turkey that had become the epicenter of migrant arrivals to Europe. In 2015 , when Kurdish-Syrian toddler Aylan Kurdi washed up drowned on a Turkish beach, global attention turned to Lesbos and the NGO presence on the island soared. Frontex personnel filled restaurants, along with members of the Greek Coast Guard and army. States began arresting humanitarian activists. The crackdown in Greek-Turkish waters, said Lopes, made the far more dangerous Central Mediterranean route, one of the deadliest in the world, much more popular. The EU, the Italian foreign ministry, the Maltese maritime authorities, the Italian Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre and the Libyan Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre did not respond to requests for comment from In These Times, nor did Israeli Aerospace Industry or Airbus. The Ocean Viking, pictured above, is equipped with radar, a small hospital and living quarters for its crew of rescuers. The movements of NGO rescue boats like this have become increasingly restricted after Italy introduced new hard-line, anti-immigration legislation. Photo by Ali Arkady As his rescuers recount it, Daniel arrived alone at the rocky shore in Sabratha, Libya, last spring, ready to cross the Mediterranean to Europe, as merchants and sailors had done for thousands of years. He had already travelled more than 1 , 200 miles from his home in the closed dictatorship of Eritrea. On May 20 , 2025 , there was a storm brewing out beyond the oil rigs, as 245 passengers clambered aboard two 23 -foot wooden boats, one painted bright blue. Daniel was last to board the boat with a tall, jutting prow, a weak engine and not enough fuel. As the passengers reached the high seas that night, waves crashed against the skiff, upsetting fuel cans. Passenger vomit mixed with urine, kerosene and seawater, creating a noxious slurry below deck in the tightly packed hold. The next morning, the storm worsened, and a passenger sent out a phone alert. The Italian Coast Guard rescued one boat but did not return for Daniel’s. The Libyan Coast Guard sent a boat from Zawiyah, 30 miles west of Tripoli, to intercept the migrants and return them to Libya, but they hit bad weather, Ocean Viking crewmembers later told me, forcing the group to turn back. As Daniel’s boat drifted away from the drowning man, the crew of a large merchant ship trying to rescue them sent an urgent mayday signal about possible people in the water, requesting assistance and guidance on what to do with the 35 people they had managed to rescue before the migrant boat pulled away. The merchant vessel, the MV Bobic, registered in the Marshall Islands, turned south to Libya to return the rescued migrants. The NGO Alarm Phone, which relays messages to rescue boats and authorities from shipwrecked migrants, informed the merchant ship that it was illegal to return migrants to Libya, where there is a credible risk of torture and abuse. A deputy commissioner of maritime affairs for the Republic of the Marshall Islands suggested the merchant vessel go to Tunisia, then asked Libya to take responsibility for the decision, according to emails published by Alarm Phone. Merchant ships operate on strict margins and any rescue will cost crucial days sailing time for the captain and ship’s company. That evening, a relative of one of the rescued migrants told Alarm Phone that the 35 people who made it onboard the Bobic had been taken to Libya’s al-Nasr detention center in Zawiyah, notorious for torture . The Ocean Viking was on its way, but was still returning from dropping off migrants shipwrecked near Tunisia — including Ahmed, Josef and Helen, whom I’d met — in northern Italy. If it hadn’t been compelled to drop them off first, as the new regulations dictated, it could have been closer to Daniel’s boat and more people may have survived. On May 25 , 2025 , the evening after the MV Bobic rescue, another merchant ship, the MV Eco One, approached the 81 migrants, including Daniel, still adrift. The Eco One was roughly six times the size of their boat, but the survivors were so exhausted and scared of the bruising storm that they apparently lost fear of other threats and bravely tried to approach the ship’s colossal, metal hull. The crew of the Eco One threw down a small rope with a ring at the end. The migrants rushed to climb aboard, and in the scrum, four people fell into the water, Daniel told the Ocean Viking’s crew. The Eco’s crew threw life rings down into the swell to catch the fallen. Two survivors were pulled from the water and hauled back onto the wooden boat, but the other two — one man of around 25 and a child of 13 — were too far away, according to Daniel’s account. “ We [sailed] away from the second ship as we saw too many people falling down. We were scared because of what happened with the rope. Everyone went for themselves,” Daniel told the Ocean Viking crew. During the rescue attempt, the crew of the Eco One managed to recover 26 people from the boat before aborting the rescue due to the storm. The Italian maritime authorities then told the Eco One to take the survivors to Lampedusa and rescue the remaining shipwrecked people once weather conditions allowed. The Ocean Viking, then about an hour away, also received the order. Neither the deputy commissioner of maritime affairs for the Republic of the Marshall Islands nor the management companies of the MV Bobic and Eco One responded to requests for comment. At this point, Daniel and his fellow migrants still caught in the storm saw what could be another ship in the distance — possibly an oil rig resupply vessel, its deck lit up like a Christmas tree, so bright that ​ “ it blinded us,” according to Daniel. They called out to the ship, asking anyone on board to help them, but ​ “ no one listened,” he recalled. He went down below deck into the cramped hold and tried not to think about the storm, or the juddering prow threatening to break, or the lack of fuel, or the sick passengers. When the Ocean Viking approached Daniel’s boat, it was midnight and the sea was black. A video of the rescue shows a headlamp jutting over bouncing, black waves, until the lights of the oil tanker that had passed by appeared in the distance. In the foreground is the tiny migrant boat, spinning on the swell. The Ocean Viking rescuers couldn’t see anyone out on deck, but as they drew closer, a man shouted out, ​ “ there are more of us down below.” As the Ocean Viking’s lifeboats finally reached the skiff, Aquilino noticed a strong smell of diesel. Many of the passengers were in various states of shock, he said, and most of them were sheltering below deck in the space filled with water. The women below deck ​ “ were not okay,” said Lopes. The next day, he recalled seeing one woman whose eyes were rolling back in her head. ​ “ She was not there,” Lopes said. Aquilino described a woman who had fallen in the water as appearing to have just come ​ “ back from the dead.” In the aftermath of the rescue, she cried out for her brother, who may have been one of the men who drowned, according to Aquilino. The survivors were so traumatized that it was difficult for the rescuers to understand exactly what happened. A group of migrants sleep aboard the Ocean Viking in May 2025. They were among 276 people who were rescued over the course of a single day after being shipwrecked off the coast of Tunisia during a storm. Photo by Ali Arkady As European rights groups, humanitarian organizations, and lawyers push for accountability, the violent reality continues at sea. In early 2017 , Italy signed an anti-migration deal with Libya, including significant support in the form of training and resources for the Libyan Coast Guard. Later that year, the Italian government invited Abd al-Rahman Milad— a notorious human trafficker as well as a chief of the Libyan Coast Guard — to Sicily to discuss anti-migrant coordination , even though a UN report determined Milad and his unit were responsible for shootings at sea. This model of cutting deals in exchange for a reduction in migration flows is defined by a lack of a unified EU strategy that will ​ “ at best sustain the status quo,” said Mark Micallef, a director at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. ​ “ This is more or less the model that Gaddafi himself had established, an extortion-type model where ​ ‘ you give me money or I will send more migrants,’” Micallef continued. ​ “ What we see now is the proliferation of that model across Libya.” But not only have these deals failed to prevent migrant flows, they are also driving instability, according to experts. In Libya, human smuggling and trafficking industries are ​ “ putting money in the hands of militias that are then in a much better position to undermine the political process and the peace process,” according to Micallef. A better approach, he said, should include a greater emphasis on law enforcement, actually going after high-level criminals, alongside a visa scheme and refugee track, as well as ​ “ red lines” for partnership countries. ​ “ You need to be able to say actually this is a line we won’t cross,” he said. Allison West of the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights said pushbacks at sea to Libya mark the beginning of ​ “ the severe deprivation of liberty as a crime against humanity.” “ People are deprived of their liberty at sea and then taken straight into detention centers in a systematic manner,” West said. Referring to EU deals with Libya, she added that this process ​ “ establishes a pathway for individual criminal responsibility for high-ranking officials in charge of the policies that make this whole system possible.” Following a similar attempt six years earlier, the submission names the European officials as co-perpetrators in the deaths of 25,000 asylum seekers, as well as abuses against some 150,000 survivors “abducted and forcibly transferred to Libya, where they were detained, tortured, raped, and enslaved.” When Italian authorities control a rescue at sea, West said, this can be enough ​ “ to establish the co-perpetration” of crimes against humanity, provided migrants are subsequently pushed back to Libyan detention sites, where some become victims of enforced disappearances. Because these disappearances occur with the direct knowledge or acquiescence of state authorities, West added, ​ “ they also impose a number of positive obligations on states to search for, to investigate and to continue until the whereabouts of the person are actually found and known.” In an October 2025 submission to the International Criminal Court, a group of lawyers accused 120 European leaders of committing crimes against humanity alongside Libyan suspects. Following a similar attempt six years earlier, the submission names the European officials as co-perpetrators in the deaths of 25 , 000 asylum seekers, as well as abuses against some 150 , 000 survivors ​ “ abducted and forcibly transferred to Libya, where they were detained, tortured, raped, and enslaved.” Now, even the rescuers are coming under attack. Humanitarian vessels threaten the financial and logistical arrangements between the EU and Libya. For the militias running Libyan detention centers, these ships undermine the cyclical business model of extortion. West describes the violence directed at rescue boats as ​ “ a maritime front of this broader containment policy.” In August 2025 , the Ocean Viking came under heavy machine gun fire , reportedly from Libyan forces sailing a vessel gifted by Italy. The attack destroyed the Viking’s antennas, broke four windows and damaged three rescue boats and rescue equipment, grounding the ship and stopping all rescues for about four months. Aquilino, on board at the time, said the gunfire was intense. He heard the metallic clink of bullets hitting the roof, windows and doors of the bridge. “ We were all falling down on the floor,” he said, hiding and ​ “ waiting for it to finish.” By early morning on May 26 , all 53 survivors remaining in Daniel’s boat after the Eco One rescue made it on board the Ocean Viking. The Italians instructed the ship to drop them off in Livorno, Tuscany, approximately 560 miles away. Five survivors were medically evacuated, including a teenager whose skin had been burned by exposure to fuel in the hold of the boat, as well as her baby. Along with her went a man with a broken arm who fell while attempting to climb the rope during the first rescue and a woman who Aquilino said inhaled too much seawater, likely developing a lung infection. Next, the Ocean Viking dropped off the dozens of lone children, along with the handful still with family members, in Sicily, following an appeal from the NGO to the island’s public prosecutor. But the Italian authorities did not allow the remaining 13 survivors to disembark there. Instead, the Ocean Viking traveled north to Livorno. On May 29 , the Ocean Viking dropped off the remaining passengers. The original group of 117 migrants had been split among three ports and one Libyan detention center. Three had drowned. According to the rescuers, on arrival in Italy, security officials were there to question the survivors. Angelo Selim, the Ocean Viking’s search and rescue coordinator, who later spoke to me on the phone, detailed the harrowing journey of the survivors: the separation across distant ports, untreated injuries and the inhospitable welcome they received in Europe. He described the companions they had watched drown along the way. “ We don’t consider these people as humans,” he said. ​ “ The only reason this can happen is because we dehumanize these people. Until the last day, they suffer from our lack of empathy.” Free for any DSA or Union member Get 10 print issues of our award-winning, worker-first journalism here!

articles.title: Train Crashes Destroyed Their Towns. Will Yours Be Next?
articles.content: Nearly 10 years before the train derailment and subsequent chemical disaster in East Palestine, Ohio, the town of Lac-Mégantic, Quebec experienced one of the deadliest rail disasters in North America. On July 6 , 2013 , a runaway train derailed in the center of town, leveling buildings and dumping millions of tons of crude oil onto the surrounding area. 47 people were killed in the explosion. In July , Maximillian Alvarez and Dr. Nicole Fabricant sat down with a panel of guests from East Palestine and Lac-Mégantic to discuss what happens when your town becomes a sacrifice zone and how residents can join together to fight back against the corporations responsible. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Maximillian Alvarez: Welcome, everyone, to Working People, a podcast about the lives, jobs, dreams, and struggles of the working class today. My name is Maximillian Alvarez. I’m the host of this podcast, and I’m also the editor in chief and co-executive director of the Real News Network. Dr. Nicole Fabricant: I’m Dr. Nicole Fabricant. I teach anthropology at Towson University. I’ve been working for 15 years in an overburdened area of Baltimore, a community named Curtis Bay, where [many] toxic, polluting industries are housed in one residential area. This zip code has some of the highest rates of respiratory illness in the entire country. Maximillian Alvarez: For the past three years on this show, along with covering other essential working-class stories and labor issues, we’ve been speaking regularly with working people in Ohio and Pennsylvania, whose lives have been forever changed by the Norfolk Southern train derailment and chemical disaster [in East Palestine] in early February of 2023 . Dr. Nicole Fabricant: But before East Palestine, there was Lac-Mégantic, one of the deadliest rail disasters in North American history. On July 6 , 2013 , an unattended 74 -car freight train carrying crude oil rolled downhill and derailed in the town center of Lac-Mégantic, Quebec. A fire broke out on the lead locomotive while the train was parked. Firefighters responded, and in the process of fighting the fire, shut down the engine, inadvertently disabling the air brakes that had been keeping the train stationary. After they left, the train began to roll, gathering speed over 11 kilometers of downhill track before derailing at a curve in Lac-Mégantic’s downtown core. The resulting explosions and fire were enormous, destroying 40 buildings in the town center, including a popular bar that was full of patrons at the time — 47 people were killed. About 2000 residents had to be evacuated, and a large portion of Lac-Mégantic’s downtown was obliterated. It remains a stark example of how these cascading institutional failures, regulatory, corporate, and operational, can lead to catastrophic consequences. With the help from the incredible folks at Railroad Workers United (RWU), we’ve brought together a truly historic panel of residents who survived the Lac-Mégantic disaster in Canada and the East Palestine rail disaster here in the United States. Robert Bellefleur: My name is Robert Bellefleur. I am the spokesperson for the [Citizens’ Coalition for Railroad Safety]… which was created in 2015 following the Lac-Mégantic tragedy. Gilbert Carette: Hi, my name is Gilbert Carette, Lac-Mégantic resident and member of the Lac-Mégantic Citizens’ Coalition for Railroad Safety. We started this coalition, and we’ve been working hard for the safety in this town, and we want the rail out of Lac-Mégantic. Gilles Fluet: My name is Gilles Fluet, and I was an eyewitness to the arrival of the ghost train in Lac-Mégantic. Anne-Marie Saint-Cerny: My name is Anne-Marie Saint-Cerny. I’ve been an activist against contamination in sacrifice zones … for more than 30 years. I was in Lac-Mégantic five days after the tragedies because I understood the intense contamination that would have happened there, and there I decided to go to the bottom of that to name the people responsible [for] what happened. Jami Wallace: My name is Jami Wallace, and I’m from East Palestine, Ohio. I lived within the one-mile zone when the Norfolk Southern train derailed in my community. I subsequently found out that my house was contaminated, and if we had blindly listened to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and went back into our house, that great harm or death could have came to my family. Ever since then, I’ve been fighting. Christina Siceloff: My name is Christina Siceloff, and I am from Darlington, Pennsylvania, and live about six miles from where the train derailed in East Palestine, Ohio. After the derailment, there was a following vent and burn that occurred, and most of the plume from that had gone over my home and the surrounding areas around East Palestine, and have been dealing with health issues in my family ever since. Gilles Fluet: Continuing from the explosion in the city and train derailment, I’d never been through anything like that before. I felt like I was in a bad dream. I also realized later that it was frowned upon to name the real, potential culprits. Robert Bellefleur: I saw the plumes of smoke, and I have to admit it was surreal — it was as if Lac-Mégantic had just been bombed. It was outsiders who came to manage the crisis in Lac-Mégantic — not even the city council was involved in the decision making. We were stripped of our powers as citizens and as a community to the benefit of the governments, who did everything they could to stall the situation, hide the real causes, and exclude us from the important decisions that needed to be made. Maximillian Alvarez: And Jami, Christina, for our guests in Canada and for folks listening to this, could you just remind them what actually happened to your towns and how you experienced it firsthand? Jami Wallace: On February 3 of 2023 , a Norfolk Southern train derailed in East Palestine. [Norfolk Southern] wanted to get the railroad back up and running, so they did a vent and burn where they caught these tankers of chemicals on fire. It went from one tanker to five tankers of vinyl chloride that they ended up exploding. The mushroom cloud looked like an atomic bomb was dropped. We were told less than 48 hours that it was safe to go home, that there were no high levels of chemicals, and that everything was great. I didn’t have to be a scientist — I didn’t have to be smart to look at that plume and know that less than 48 hours [later] they couldn’t tell us with certainty that it was safe to go home. As soon as people went back home, the symptoms started: the nosebleeds, the rashes, the coughing and respiratory issues. They gaslit us, tried to tell us that it was stress, that it was mental mass psychosis. We have 64 people in our community with cancer now. It’s amazing when you hear these other stories and you hear all the same things happening, and this is in a different country, but it’s the same playbook. Christina Siceloff: When everybody was being told that everything was fine, the air was fine, the water was fine, we were seeing thousands of fish popping up in the creeks that were dead. So, I went to the creeks and saw the sheen that was left from the chemicals that were in the water that traveled down to the Ohio River, and that was the start of me going to the creeks for the next two and a half years to show that the government was saying one thing, and we were experiencing another. Robert Bellefleur: The thing is, in Lac-Mégantic, we felt that control was coming entirely from outside, they sent us press spokespeople from the various governments to control the message, to calm the public, to prevent them from rebelling. However, when we asked them to set up a public inquiry commission, the answer was a categorical no, so we felt manipulated and divided by the government forces that had taken control of the situation. We, as citizens, decided in 2015 to form a citizens’ coalition for rail safety because the transport of oil and hazardous materials had resumed six months after the tragedy. I went to inspect the railroad tracks surrounding Lac-Mégantic, and found that the rails were still in very poor condition, even though hazardous materials — 10 x more dangerous than the shale oil that had set the town ablaze — were now being transported on them. In reality, Lac-Mégantic has experienced three disasters. First, the train derailment. Following that, the complete demolition of the downtown area against the wishes of the residents. And third, they succeeded in dividing the community over the bypass project. They turned it into a project of social division, and there are friends and families in the region who haven’t spoken to each other since then. Anne-Marie Saint-Cerny: The authorities that were in charge of safeties, environmental authorities, and all that — they were all absent. If there are no community surveillance, if there are no communities implicated, there is nothing. I saw that for the first time in Mégantic, which was the biggest massive death of modern Canada… there were no authorities to keep the people safe. Jami Wallace: We learned very quickly in East Palestine that no one else was going to fight for us if we didn’t fight for ourselves. When you’re exposed to these type of chemicals, we know from every other chemical disaster it can take years before these things show up in our communities. The derailment itself was a disaster. The vent and burn was a disaster. The flooding that occurred in our creeks afterwards, another disaster. And then that whole economic recovery, that’s another disaster. You should see what it’s done to our small community that I always thought was tight-knit. We always looked out for each other, but the focus on the economy has overshadowed any focus whatsoever on human health. I literally was getting goosebumps on my arms listening to the similarities, and that’s where we all need to come together, because it’s not just about East Palestine. These disasters are so much bigger than that. Maximillian Alvarez: [What] have these whole awful, unforgivable, life-changing experiences taught you that you most want to communicate to others out there who are going through this now, or who may go through it one day? Anne-Marie Saint-Cerny: These are industrial tragedies that are going to go on exploding again and again… All of us together, we have to never surrender. We have to hold the line — and how do we do that? We expose the fact. Facts will come and will make themselves known, and people will eventually change. Jami Wallace: We need to take all these fighters from all these different communities and bring our voices together. The bigger our voices can be, the louder we can be, the better the chances that will be heard. Maximillian Alvarez: All right, gang. That’s gonna wrap things up for us today. From Lac-Mégantic to East Palestine and beyond… It’s clear that corporations and our governments are turning more and more of our communities into sacrifice zones, and more and more of us are being set up for sacrifice. All of us have a role to play in this fight, and we here at Working People, the Real News Network, and In These Times will continue our work to lift up the voices and stories of the people like you who are on the front lines of this fight, and to bring people together on and offline. This episode of the Working People Podcast was published on July 6 . Free for any DSA or Union member Get 10 print issues of our award-winning, worker-first journalism here!

articles.title: The Big Idea: Winning
articles.content: In These Times is proud to be independent, pro-labor and anti-fascist. Support our work today and help left-wing journalism thrive. verb 1 . to obtain by work 2 . to be the victor Winning elections has, historically, been difficult for socialists in the United States. Less than 1 % of Congress identifies as democratic socialists. Just two years ago, the Left suffered high-profile losses after a consortium of corporations and pro-Israel donors spent an unprecedented amount of money in congressional primaries to unseat former Reps. Cori Bush (D-Mo.) and Jamaal Bowman (D-N.Y.). So when on June 23 , just six months into Zohran Mamdani’s tenure as mayor of New York City, his entire endorsed slate of democratic socialist candidates, including two now-likely congresswomen, won their New York primaries, the national press took notice, and many members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) looked up from their billionaire-controlled social media feeds with a revelation. Winning feels great. Let’s keep doing it. Let’s run the numbers. The day Mamdani launched his campaign in October 2024 , the New York City chapter of DSA had 5 , 910 members. Today, there are more than 15 , 000 — thousands more people willing to make dues payments to propel the socialist movement forward. The trajectory is similar for national DSA. Some 50 , 000 members in 2024 have grown to nearly 130 , 000 as of August, and over 12 , 000 of those members have joined since the June NYC primaries. The DSA chapter in Washington, D.C., meanwhile, gained more than 1 , 000 dues-paying members during Janeese Lewis George’s successful bid for mayor, and chapters in Denver, Colo. and Madison, Wis. have similarly surged in the process of backing Melat Kiros’s victorious Congressional primary campaign and Francesca Hong in her ongoing bid for governor, respectively. Winning means growing, and growing quickly. Plus, Mamdani has already proven democratic socialist governance can deliver non-electoral victories for working people. Most notably, in June, his coalition won a rent freeze for over 2 million NYC rent-stabilized tenants. That’s millions who can now say their lives were materially improved by a democratic socialist. So, why not win? Fine, winning rocks. When’s the next one? Democratic socialists are on the ballot from now until November — from Hong in Wisconsin to Oliver Larkin running for Congress in Florida to Nithya Raman running for mayor of Los Angeles. But perhaps Mamdani himself said it best on the eve of his slate’s decisive victory. ​ “ When does the race for 2028 begin?” Mamdani asked his growing army of DSA members. ​ “ It starts now.” Free for any DSA or Union member Get 10 print issues of our award-winning, worker-first journalism here!
