articles.title: Five Books About Imperialism
articles.author: Vivek Chibber
articles.content: Marxist Theories of Imperialism: A Critical SurveyAnthony Brewer1980There is a wide range of literature theorizing imperialism, and the best place to start is an overview that is judicious, encompassing, and careful. Brewer’s book is that. It covers not only the classical theories of Vladimir Lenin and Rosa Luxemburg but also the postwar theories, like the unequal exchange arguments of Giovanni Arrighi, Immanuel Wallerstein, and Samir Amin and dependency theory. Brewer is good on all of these, laying out what each theory claims and subjecting it to serious critical scrutiny. Any socialist who reads this book will come away literate in the broad landscape of Marxist theorizing on empire.From Value to Uneven Development: Selected Writings by John Weeks in the Marxist TraditionJohn Weeks, ed. Ben Fine, Simon Mohun, and Alfredo Saad-Filho2020The most astute and penetrating critic of the postwar economic theories of imperialism, Weeks was one of the leading Marxist economists of his generation and spent years studying the empirical realities of the Global South, particularly in Africa and Latin America. He was therefore deeply committed to building a theory that captured those dynamics. His selected writings present the best sympathetic critique of Wallerstein and the dependency school available anywhere.Britain’s Imperial Century, 1815–1914Ronald Hyam1976Hyam’s book is the finest single-volume account of British imperial expansion, covering the full sweep from 1815 to 1914. It went through three editions; the third, from Palgrave Macmillan in 2002, strikes the best balance between covering the high years of empire and engaging with the analytical debates that surround them. Hyam is equally good at narrating the story of expansion and pausing to examine the forces and contradictions that drove it. For any reader who wants to understand what British imperialism was, how it worked, and why it took the forms it did, this is indispensable.Mammon and the Pursuit of Empire: The Political Economy of British Imperialism, 1860–1912Lance E. Davis and Robert A. Huttenback1986Alongside the narrative history, you need to understand the economic dynamics of colonialism. What were the costs of colonial empires to the metropole, and what was actually produced by the colonies? Davis and Huttenback’s book is the most careful study of the data on the profits of imperialism ever produced, and its findings are arresting. Empire was likely a net drain on the British economy rather than an engine of growth. No serious student of imperialism can afford to ignore it.The Enigma of Colonialism: British Policy in West AfricaAnne Phillips1989The final piece of the puzzle is understanding how empire consolidated itself in the Global South, and the best guide to that question is this short and beautifully written book. Phillips studies the onset and dynamics of British Empire in West Africa from the 1880s into the 1940s. Where thinkers like Luxemburg had predicted that colonialism would commodify the economy, dissolve traditional social relations, and integrate the colonized into a market for British goods, Phillips shows that it did the opposite. It consolidated peasant property and put the brakes on capitalist development. The reason was the political logic of colonial rule itself. British capitalists were never particularly interested in West Africa, and the colonial state’s overriding need was stability, not transformation.

articles.title: Agitslop
articles.content: In 1872, George Crofutt, a publisher of travel guides advertising the American West, commissioned a painting from the German-born John Gast: an idyllic depiction of westward-bound American pioneers. Floating above them is Columbia, the female personification of the United States that inspired the following decade’s Statue of Liberty, bearing a textbook in one hand and a telegraph wire in the other. In her wake come the hallmarks of American modernization that would lend the painting its name: railroad, ships, and farmers, all illuminated by a rising sun marching inexorably westward across the sky. This is perhaps the single image most associated with manifest destiny, which held that the United States had a divine right to occupy the whole of North America — at the expense, of course, of the Native Americans who already inhabited those lands. John Gast’s American Progress (1872) American Progress (1872) is just one of the propaganda images repurposed by the Department of Homeland Security for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) recruitment in 2025. “A Heritage to be proud of, a Homeland worth Defending,” reads a caption accompanying the image, posted to X. Other images shared by DHS include Thomas Kinkade’s Morning Pledge (2015), which depicts an idyllic small town complete with mid-century cars, and Morgan Weistling’s A Prayer for a New Life (2020), which shows a pioneer couple admiring their newborn infant on the frontier — as well as a large number of seemingly AI-rendered riffs on World War I and World War II military recruitment posters. So many themes are invoked simultaneously in this campaign that its message becomes almost incoherent. In fact, what unites the images shared by DHS is the history of US imperialism — its excesses now directed inward against Americans at home. Go West, Young Man Morgan Weistling’s A Prayer for a New Life (2020) Image shared by @DHSgov As with Gast’s American Progress , many of the propaganda posts shared by DHS invoke the image of westward expansion. Weistling’s A Prayer for a New Life depicts the interior of a covered wagon, in which a pair of American pioneers welcome a child who has been born in the process of migrating west. In the distance, another covered wagon is visible, and beyond that, vast emptiness. That same emptiness foregrounds Uncle Sam in the potentially AI-rendered “America Needs You” poster shared by DHS: the continent is depicted bereft of indigenous civilization, occupied only by European settlers. In the “America Needs You” poster, Uncle Sam stands beside a signpost indicating that both “homeland” and “opportunity” lie in the West. WWI Redux James Montgomery Flagg’s “Wake Up, America!” (1917) Image shared by @DHSgov Vincent Aderente and Frances Adams Halsted’s “Columbia Calls” (1916) Image shared by @DHSgov Some of the images shared by DHS for ICE recruitment ape the aesthetics of World War I posters, including Flagg’s “Wake Up, America!” and Aderente and Halsted’s “Columbia Calls,” both of which feature Columbia on the front lines of global conflict. In the former, Columbia is imperiled by storm clouds gathering on the horizon, while in the latter, she prepares to march forth from the United States to military glory abroad. Together, the two images tell a story of American neutrality that gives way to intervention only under duress — a narrative belied by US imperial activity in the years leading up to World War I, which saw the United States acquire Hawaii, the Philippines, Puerto Rico, Eastern Samoa, Guantanamo, Guam, and the Panama Canal Zone and launch military interventions in Nicaragua, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Cuba, Panama, Mexico, and Honduras.

articles.title: Raphäel Glucksmann, a Hawk in Progressive Clothing
articles.author: Eldar Mamedov
articles.content: On August 23, Raphaël Glucksmann, the French essayist and member of the European Parliament (MEP), officially announced what had long been an open secret: his candidacy for the 2027 presidential election as a standard-bearer of the French center left. To my eyes, his candidacy is a disaster in the making and, in fact, a story I’ve already seen unfold from close range. I first encountered him not in Paris elite circles but in the wreckage of Georgian hubris, back in 2013, when I visited that country as part of the delegation of the European Parliament’s foreign affairs committee. Glucksmann, then in his early thirties, was suave, articulate, and utterly convinced of his own righteousness. He was then serving as a foreign adviser to Mikheil Saakashvili, the mercurial Georgian president whose adventurism , encouraged by the George W. Bush administration, had culminated in the 2008 war with Russia and Russian forces advancing deep into Georgia . Glucksmann spoke of Western integration with the fervor of a true believer . He did not speak of the limits of Georgian power and the precariousness of the country’s geopolitical position, or the cost of Saakashvili’s recklessness in ignoring it. Years later, long after he had swapped Tbilisi for Brussels, and once it had become impossible to ignore the extent of democratic degradation under Saakashvili, Glucksmann’s loyalty to his former patron remained undiminished. Not only had he continued to defend his record, but he also actively lobbied his own political group in the EU Parliament, the center-left Progressive Alliance, to sever all ties with the ruling Georgian Dream party, which had just defeated Saakashvili’s United National Movement at the ballot box. The irony was lost on no one who’d been paying attention. Glucksmann, the self-professed progressive, aligned himself with the right-wing European People’s Party (EPP), which had made Saakashvili’s defense and alliance with his nationalist party their top priority in relations with Georgia. For the EPP, this was an exercise in political tribalism thinly disguised under rhetoric about “democracy.” Glucksmann’s joining of the EPP on Georgia was not a corrective, a response to the Georgian Dream’s alleged retreat from democratic principles. On the contrary, his maneuvers took place long before the controversial foreign agents law was adopted in Georgia in 2022, in a move that eventually became a rallying cry for Western critics of Georgian Dream. But it is worth asking how much Glucksmann’s own misguided activism contributed to the very outcome — Georgia’s stalled EU bid — that he now decries. The foreign agents law , when it came, was in part a product of the polarization that Glucksmann had done much to deepen. A Hawk in Progressive Clothing My first encounter with Glucksmann in Tbilisi might have been a distant memory, had I not found myself, years later, working in the same institution where he’d made his political home. In 2019, he had been elected as a MEP for his center-left outfit Place Publique and joined the Progressive Alliance in the European Parliament. At the time, I was serving as a foreign policy staffer for this same group. Back in the mid-2000s, I’d been drawn to it by the belief that internationalism, human rights, and European cooperation could coexist with strategic restraint and skepticism toward military power. The disappointment of that belief would eventually drive me away from it. This was not the result of any sudden conversion to the right, but the growing decay of the European center-left (“socialist”) tradition itself: foreign policy had become an empty vessel for self-congratulatory virtue signaling. I found myself increasingly closer to the old-fashioned realists — and, on questions of individual liberty, to libertarians — than to the progressives with whom I had once worked. Glucksmann was, to me, an embodiment of that decay. He had shed his Georgian skin and donned the mantle of progressive savior, but the underlying instinct was unchanged: a hawk preaching liberal values at home while clamoring for confrontation abroad. One memorable episode came in 2022, when the football World Cup was to be held in Qatar. The Progressive Alliance descended on it like a ton of bricks — not only over its labor rights record, which was a legitimate concern in its own right, but over gay rights and, heaven forbid, restricting alcohol consumption at stadiums. At a group meeting in Strasbourg, before the vote on the resolution condemning Qatar in November 2022, an experienced MEP, then chair of the parliament’s human rights subcommittee, objected that denouncing countries was not always the best way to promote reform. Otherwise, she argued, “as an example, we’ll have to also remove the GSP [Generalised Scheme of Preferences]+ trade arrangement with Pakistan for its human rights shortcomings. Is that what we want?” Glucksmann’s eyes lit up. “Yes,” he said. If consistency demanded sanctioning more countries over their human rights record, then so be it, he argued. I sat dumbfounded. If it were up to him, I thought, the EU would soon be at war with the entire world, except, perhaps, Canada and Norway. It was not only in committee rooms that I witnessed this instinct. On more than one occasion, his assistant called my office, demanding to know why the progressives were not supporting ultra-hawkish amendments on Russia (appended to already strongly worded motions) tabled by the hard-right European Conservatives and Reformists. The man presenting himself as the future of the French center left was pressuring progressives to vote alongside parties like Poland’s Law and Justice or the Sweden Democrats , whose nationalist and socially conservative politics otherwise put them at odds with everything Glucksmann claims to represent. On Russia, however, they were allies of convenience. Anyone who hesitated risked being treated as a mere “ Putin appeaser .” Blind Spots For all his fervor on Russia and China, where he is among the most vocal hawks in the European Parliament, Glucksmann’s moral compass has a curious blind spot. A January 2026 resolution on Iran provided one example. Glucksmann broke with his own group by abstaining on an amendment reaffirming Iranian sovereignty in determining its own political system and leadership, while voting against criticisms of Israel and calls for de-escalation. A politician who lectured countries such as Pakistan and Qatar on human rights and social mores and demanded a Europe-wide confrontation with Moscow and Beijing was reluctant to apply the same political pressure to Israel. To be fair, the picture is not entirely one-sided. In November 2024, Glucksmann coauthored a Le Monde op-ed with Daniel Cohn-Bendit that condemned Israel’s government’s war in Gaza and Lebanon in strong terms. They described the Israeli conduct as a violation of the laws of war and argued that the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant was not antisemitic. Yet the framing of his critique of Israel was telling. By assigning primary causal and moral agency to Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran, Glucksmann treats Israeli policies — occupation, settlements, apartheid — as aggravating factors rather than foundational drivers of the conflict. The occupation and settlements are mentioned but appear as contextual grievances (“the permanent extension of settlements is unbearable”) rather than as the structural engine that perpetuates violence. The same selectivity appears in his response to the US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February 2026. Following the attacks, Glucksmann expressed solidarity with Iranians fighting the Islamic Republic, warned of regional escalation, invoked the Iraq war and questioned whether Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu could be trusted to relieve the suffering of the Iranian people. But he conspicuously stopped short of explicitly condemning the strikes themselves as unlawful. The question is no longer whether an action is legal or prudent but whether it furthers his goal of regime change in Iran. This pattern of selective indignation extends to other areas of his performance. In the European Parliament, Glucksmann secured for himself the position of the chair of the newly established Special Committee on Foreign Interference. From that perch, he set his sights, predictably, on a handful of familiar adversaries: Russia and China foremost among them. While his views on Russia were well known, he also targeted China by notably cultivating ties with Taiwan and seeking the recognition of China’s treatment of Uighurs as genocide. Yet this narrow framing conveniently overlooked a glaring reality closer to home. In a recent interview , François Fillon, a Gaullist conservative and prime minister in 2007–2012, put it bluntly: “The most significant foreign interference” that Europe faces is “first and foremost, that of the Americans,” adding that “the Americans are constantly interfering in the organization of European countries.” Fillon elaborated further on “a particularly insidious mechanism that allows them to sanction Western companies. That is how, for example, [French bank] BNP was ordered to pay several billion in fines to America. That is how America can sanction a Western company like Airbus, for instance, to give an advantage to Boeing.” Fillon referred to specifically was a record $9 billion fine BNP Paribas had to pay in 2014 for allegedly breaking US sanctions against trade with Iran and Cuba. We all knew it, but it’s quite remarkable for someone of Fillon’s stature to say it out loud. The contrast with Glucksmann’s narrow focus is instructive. For a politician who has made a career of denouncing foreign influence, the one form of interference that is most pervasive — American economic and legal coercion, the weaponization of the dollar, the extraterritorial reach of US sanctions — is curiously absent from his crusade. To be sure, Glucksmann does occasionally condemn US interference — but only insofar as it emanates from the Trump administration and MAGA-aligned far-right networks that he already opposes on ideological grounds. This is the interference he is comfortable naming, because it fits his preexisting political narrative. What he consistently fails to acknowledge is the normalized interference that long predates Trumpism: the structural, systemic, bipartisan exercise of American power that Fillon described. It’s precisely this kind of interference that Glucksmann refuses to confront. The French Neocon Ascendancy No isolated phenomenon, Glucksmann’s recent prominence illustrates a broader, troubling shift in French foreign policy: the rise of a new French neoconservatism. This neoconservatism à la française is not simply a US transplant. It does not derive from the Cold War anti-communism of Irving Kristol or Commentary’ s crusade for American global hegemony. Rather, it has its own genealogy and its own distinctly French intellectual texture. Its roots go back to the nouveaux philosophes : a group including Raphaël’s father, André Glucksmann, as well as Bernard-Henri Lévy and Pascal Bruckner, among others. These former leftists broke with Marxism after Alexander Solzhenitsyn’s revelations about the gulag and embraced an increasingly militant “anti-totalitarianism.” They retained a culturally liberal sensibility — opposition to clericalism, defense of secularism, suspicion of traditional authority — while abandoning much of the Old Left’s skepticism toward military power. Where the US and French variants of neoconservatism converge is in the worldview in which Western power is not merely permitted to confront tyranny but morally obliged to do so. The distinction between opposing an authoritarian regime and launching a war against it began to disappear. The pattern became unmistakable in the Balkans. The nouveaux philosophes were among the most enthusiastic French supporters of NATO’s 1999 bombing of Yugoslavia. Then came the 2003 war in Iraq, in which Paris did not participate. André Glucksmann and Pascal Bruckner were among the leading French intellectuals who openly supported the US invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein and unleashed a yearslong civil war. This is where the contrast with traditional French Gaullist tradition becomes decisive. Jacques Chirac and his foreign minister, Dominique de Villepin, had no interest in defending Saddam Hussein. They simply understood something the moral crusaders did not: removing a dictator is not the same thing as building a stable political order, and military power is no substitute for a strategy for what comes next. De Villepin’s February 2003 speech at the United Nations became the defining expression of that judgment. History was considerably kinder to the Gaullists’ judgment than to the neoconservatives’. Iraq produced precisely the kind of strategic disaster Chirac and de Villepin had warned about: the destruction of the Iraqi state, sectarian conflict, regional destabilization, and conditions in which jihadist movements could flourish. Yet such Gaullist restraint was not to last. From Sarkozy to Macron In 2007, André Glucksmann publicly endorsed right-winger Nicolas Sarkozy for president. His endorsement symbolized a broader realignment: French anti-totalitarian interventionists were finding a home around a politician determined to break with essential elements of the Gaullist tradition in favor of a more Atlanticist orientation, such as reintegrating France into NATO’s military command. Sarkozy went on to win the presidential election that year. The appointment of Bernard Kouchner as foreign minister, reportedly at the suggestion of André Glucksmann, brought the nouveaux philosophes’ humanitarian interventionism directly into the heart of French foreign policy: Kouchner, cofounder of Médecins Sans Frontières , embodied the “right to interfere” ( droit d’ingérence ) doctrine, namely the belief that humanitarian concern could and should override state sovereignty. This framing was a major break with earlier Gaullist tradition. The irony is that Kouchner’s subsequent career reveals the darker side of humanitarianism. In the years after leaving office, Kouchner became a prominent supporter of the Mujahedin-e-Khalq (MEK), a bizarre, cultish organization with a history of violence, including assassinations of US citizens and Iranian officials. Yet former humanitarian icons could embrace it because it has come to be seen as a useful instrument against the Iranian regime. Added to this was the disaster in Libya. In 2011, Bernard-Henri Lévy became one of the most visible advocates of intervention against Muammar Gaddafi. He did not single-handedly persuade Sarkozy to launch the war, but he helped accelerate recognition of the Libyan rebels and create the political narrative for intervention, and he became an influential intermediary between the insurgency and the Élysée Palace. The result was another regime change war. Under the US-British-French no-fly zone, accompanied by air strikes by these same countries, Gaddafi was toppled, and Libya collapsed into years of civil war, militia rule, arms proliferation, and regional instability. The country has still not recovered from the ensuing catastrophe. The interventionist turn did not end with Sarkozy. Under his Socialist successor, François Hollande, France pursued a notably hawkish line on Syria, backing regime change in that country. On Iran too, Paris was often more hard-line than Washington during the nuclear negotiations, with Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius demanding tougher restrictions before France ultimately signed the 2015 nuclear deal. Emmanuel Macron, who succeeded Hollande as president in 2017, occasionally mused about France’s, and Europe’s, strategic autonomy but ultimately adhered broadly to the interventionist worldview that had become a mainstay of French foreign policy, notably on Ukraine and in the Middle East . After Unipolarism Raphaël Glucksmann is the latest expression of this French interventionist tradition. His particular innovation is to turn that tradition into a defining political identity of the contemporary center left: wrapping confrontation in the language of progress and making hawkishness a test of moral seriousness. But the world he wants France to confront is no longer the unipolar world in which Western power could imagine that political will was enough to remake distant societies. It is a more fragmented, competitive, and increasingly multipolar world, in which Western coercion has limits. Glucksmann and his fellow European hawks, by contrast, are pushing for rapid EU militarization in the name of a Manichaean crusade against autocracies — casting every geopolitical rival as an existential threat. But that binary worldview is a poor compass for navigating today’s complex reality. The choice before France is therefore larger than the candidacy of one man. It is whether moralism will continue to substitute for strategy. The future belongs not to those who are most certain of their righteousness but to those capable of understanding the limits of their power.

articles.title: Arms Embargo as Class Struggle
articles.author: samuel.dibella
articles.content: On October 16, 2023, just weeks after the beginning of Israel’s intensified genocidal assault on the Gaza strip, the Palestinian General Federation of Trade Unions issued a historic call . The federation asked workers across the world to refuse to build and transport weapons for Israel, as well as to take action against complicit companies and pressure their governments to end military trade. On October 31, Belgian transport workers’ unions answered, announcing that they would not handle arms shipments to Israel . “The loading and unloading of these weapons,” they wrote , “helps to provide organisations to kill innocent people… As trade unions, we declare our solidarity with those who are campaigning for peace.” The Belgian unions have since been joined by dockworkers in Italy, France, Spain, Morocco, Greece, Sweden, and more, who have refused complicity in the supply chain of genocide and refused to handle shipments of arms, ammunition, airplane parts, and other military equipment. In Italy, general strikes have swept the country in solidarity with Palestine, as not only transport workers but all working people withhold their labor from a national and global economy that enriches war-makers with the blood of Palestinians. These workers did not wait for their governments to officially declare an arms embargo, but realized their power as laborers to enact one directly (not for nothing, many of these governments have since issued formal arms embargo legislation). Nor are these spontaneous uprisings. They are the result of long-term organizing, research, and international coordination towards collective action that is both material and symbolic, both practical and highly politicized. They are an expression of the working class’s political consciousness and autonomy, over and against capital. They are, in other words, acts of class struggle. The labor movement in the United States has been slow to follow our comrades overseas, for a variety of reasons that are too numerous and complex to treat here—decades of anti-communist repression, bourgeois cooptation, class collaboration, Zionist propaganda, and legal restrictions on strikes and other labor organizing. Despite valiant efforts like those of dockworkers in Oakland, the vision of a worker-led arms embargo has remained marginal to pro-Palestine, socialist, and labor organizing in the US. 1 The idea that American workers could leverage their collective power to directly weaken the supply chain of genocide has been widely dismissed as far-fetched and idealistic. As a result, the bulk of arms embargo campaigns in the US have hinged on making appeals directly to members of Congress; an approach that has evidently borne limited fruit. I argue here that an arms embargo campaign that centers workers as protagonists of the struggle and actively cultivates anti-imperialist consciousness in the US labor movement is an indispensable task for socialists in the present moment. It is our best chance to impede Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which continues despite the so-called “ceasefire,” as well as its campaign of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and south Lebanon. An arms embargo is also a powerful vehicle of class struggle within the US, as it requires us first to cultivate class consciousness through mapping the relations of capital and imperialism, then to act on that consciousness to seize hold of and transform those relations. Launching Break the Chain The principled actions of international workers in solidarity with Palestine inspired the formation of DSA’s national Labor for an Arms Embargo campaign (LFAE), which seeks to “organize and use [the] power [of the working class] to end the genocide of Palestinians.” I have spent the last year working on the Break the Chain campaign , a local iteration of LFAE. Break the Chain was established in NYC–DSA in June 2025 after research from the Palestinian Youth Movement revealed that New York’s airports and seaports are a major shipping hub for Israeli military cargo. In the face of these revelations, amidst a horrific livestreamed genocide that continued despite years of protest, organizers in NYC–DSA’s Anti-War Working Group felt compelled to halt the deadly shipments. They convened an organizing committee and drafted a campaign proposal, which passed a branch-level vote with overwhelming popular support to become an official chapter campaign. 2 The initial phase of the campaign was the most challenging (so far). On the surface, our demand was simple: end the transfer of arms to Israel. But who exactly could end it, and how? Should we focus on one facility, or multiple across the supply chain? Had anything like this been attempted before in New York City, or anywhere in the US? We knew from the beginning that Break the Chain would be labor-centered, but which specific workers were we trying to reach, and how? These questions opened up a period of intense research, strategizing, and debate. We gathered as much information as we could, including by talking to other organizers in our networks, and used it to create power maps. We explored many avenues that turned out to be dead ends. Eventually, after months of fact-finding and deliberation, we decided to focus our efforts on JFK airport, which is the biggest exporter of goods to Israel of any US airport or seaport, with over 20% market share, as well as an iconic and accessible location for NYC residents. Since then, we have been popularizing the demand for an arms embargo by speaking to workers and community members directly. We have volunteers go out every week to flyer, table, and canvass, to let people know about the arms shipments and invite them to join our campaign. We created a website and Instagram, and worked with our DSA-endorsed candidates and elected officials to create promotional videos for social media . And we are continuing worker outreach and training efforts, offering organizing trainings and workers’ circles for hundreds of union members who want to take action for Palestine in their local. After a year of research, mapping, flyering, tabling, one-on-ones, and (so, so many) meetings, I am more convinced than ever that the struggle for an arms embargo is not a pipe dream but one of the most important sites for socialist class struggle in the United States today. I hope the Break the Chain campaign can serve as an inspiration for other socialists, anti-imperialists, and labor organizers across the country who are ready to take up the call for an arms embargo. What Is An Arms Embargo? I should clarify briefly what I mean when I say “arms embargo,” because the term has been used with imprecision. In short, I mean nothing more or less than the total end of all military trade, including exports, imports, and transport, of material goods like weapons, ammunition, aircraft and vehicle parts, fuses, etc., as well as intelligence, research, software, and technical knowledge. 3 This definition of an arms embargo, as opposed to other important but ultimately insufficient goals like the end of US military aid to Israel, is necessary because Israel relies on the “qualitative military edge” provided by American technology to perpetrate genocide and ethnic cleansing against the Palestinian people. Israel could theoretically use its own money to purchase this equipment at full price and continue the genocide, but it could not develop the sheer productive capacity necessary to maintain military domination on its own (at least, not for a long time). The arms embargo operates within the circuit of capital—it disrupts, by definition, the existing systems of production, distribution, and consumption. Purely political demands like the end of military aid, however commendable, depend ultimately on the actions of powerful politicians. The arms embargo, on the other hand, opens up the possibility of direct, democratic intervention by the thousands of people materially implicated in the production and circulation of military goods. No collection of laypeople, however large, could simply push the figurative button to stop aid packages going from Washington to Tel Aviv. But dockworkers can refuse to load ships, cargo handlers can refuse to load airplanes, truck drivers can refuse to move containers, pilots can refuse to fly, and mechanics can refuse to repair. It is not only possible; it is happening across the world right now. This line of argumentation has earned myself and my comrades plenty of charges of naïveté. The US is too large. Union density is too low. The existing unions are too conservative . There is truth to these critiques (though I remain optimistic despite the odds). But an arms embargo campaign need not necessarily rise to the level of a general—or even a dockworkers’—strike to be a potent and necessary form of class struggle. Cognitive Mapping & Class Consciousness Class struggle requires class consciousness—an understanding of one’s position in the relations of production, of oneself as shaped by and acting within vast, powerful material systems that both place objective constraints on and create opportunities for subjective action. The economic conditions of global capitalism and its ideology of neoliberal individualism have made such an understanding exponentially more difficult. But an arms embargo campaign requires the intentional exposure of the relations that capital hides—the work of mapping power, which is simultaneously the work of mapping vulnerability. In his brilliant Postmodernism , the late Marxist theorist Fredric Jameson diagnosed an objective situation: due to the immense complexity and increasing globalization of late 20th-century capitalist systems of production, it had become more difficult for individuals to apprehend their own role in these global systems. As labor was abstracted, outsourced, and atomized, old class relations seemed to fade and disappear. Against this obfuscation of the means and relations of production—the apparent disappearance of “class” as a category can only benefit the ruling class—Jameson proposed a strategy of “cognitive mapping.” Cognitive mapping is “a pedagogical political culture which seeks to endow the individual subject with some new heightened sense of its place in the global system.” For Jameson, “cognitive mapping” is a solution to an aesthetic problem, but I have never been satisfied to render such essential work entirely unto the poet. In my work on Break the Chain, I have experienced firsthand how the practical task of mapping the supply chain is also a political act of cognitive mapping. 4 For most of us, the vast sprawl of global logistics remains abstract and only breaks through into reality at moments of crisis (who knew what the Strait of Hormuz was before it was blockaded?). But an arms embargo campaign requires us to intentionally and proactively combat that abstraction, for the simple reason that to stem the flow of military cargo, it is necessary first to know precisely where that military cargo comes from, where it goes, and how it gets there. Our investigation has uncovered, so far, 38 companies complicit in the movement of military cargo from the NYC metropolitan area to the Israeli military, with hundreds more suspected but unconfirmed. These companies are everywhere, hidden in plain sight. Many are obscure, tiny contractors that produce only one specific part, but others are household names: FedEx, Delta, and United Airlines all transport weapons and military cargo out of civilian airports. Many airlines that Americans use in their daily lives are part of the US Civil Reserve Air Fleet , a program which allows private airlines to contract with the Department of War (DoW) to provide aircraft in case of wartime emergency in exchange for receiving DoW business during “peacetime.” Our investigation is an act of cognitive mapping. It resituates the seemingly isolated and innocent activity of flying on a commercial airline in the global flow of people, goods, and capital and reattaches the subjective experience of daily life to the objective totality of capitalist production—in particular, to the historical situation of imperialist exploitation that has facilitated the genocide of the Palestinians. It is also an act of burgeoning class consciousness: to recognize oneself as belonging to the class that rides, loads, builds, fuels, directs, cleans, or flies the plane, rather than the one that profits from it and decides where it will go and what it will carry, or the one for whom the contents of its belly mean death. Collective Action Across the Map But to have a map is one thing. To use it is another. This is the real power of an arms embargo campaign: it requires the creation of a map that is not sterile and academic but living, dynamic, and burning with a call to action. The arms embargo invites us to take our complicity in the global military supply chain as the starting point of struggle, rather than as the endpoint of analysis. It not only points us towards the multiple nodes and vectors of commodity flow that capital wants so badly to hide but gives us a concrete goal that can only be achieved through collective action. Again, this collective action need not necessarily be a strike. Workers may opt to pass a resolution in their local, form an investigative committee, hold a rally, write an open letter, speak to the media, or testify at a local port authority board meeting. As we have seen with Break the Chain, the demand for an arms embargo often functions as a catalyst for unionized workers to get seriously involved in their union when before they had been passive “paper members”—it may even act as an impetus for non-union workers to unionize or form other kinds of affinity groups. Once workers realize their unique positionality and power as workers , they can begin to imagine new ways to enact material, democratic control over the conditions and products of their labor. The arms embargo campaign is also unique in the ways that it marries the practical and the political. This sets it apart from, on the one hand, “bread-and-butter” labor issues that improve workers’ lives but fail to adequately politicize those improvements and, on the other hand, abstract political claims that demand workers take this or that position without responding to the material needs of workers themselves. It is often bemoaned that socialist and anti-imperialist organizers fail to “meet workers where they’re at” and instead expect them to go from apathetic to quoting Lenin in a matter of weeks. A democratic, worker-led arms embargo campaign provides this missing link: these weapons shipments are dangerous and unfair to American workers as well as deadly to Palestinians. At JFK, for example, research from The Intercept revealed that one cargo flight bound for an Israeli weapons manufacturer contained 14 tons of nitrocellulose, a highly flammable and explosive compound used to produce ammunition. An accident could affect not only the workers handling this cargo directly, but anyone in the vicinity—nitrocellulose was responsible for a 2015 explosion in Tianjin, China , that killed 165 people, recent factory explosions in Bloomfield, CT , and Prescott, WI , and more. The demand for an arms embargo cuts across issues of safety and democracy in the workplace for domestic workers and life and dignity for people under siege in Palestine. At one stroke, it provides us the framework to understand the deep connections between our everyday lives in the US and the lives of people overseas, and the means to seize hold of and transform those connections. It challenges us to create the kind of cognitive map Jameson envisioned, and then to put that map to concrete use—not merely to describe the world, as Marx would say, but to change it. Beyond even the project of the arms embargo itself, the Break the Chain campaign has brought people together in new ways, spawning new connections and ideas about how to organize for a better world. It has not only helped empower people to become active as union members, but brought people into DSA and introduced them to or helped them to deepen their understanding of the ideas of socialism and internationalism. It has built and strengthened ties between the labor movement, the Palestine movement, and socialist organizations. At the time of this writing, three union locals have passed resolutions calling for an arms embargo at JFK, fifteen labor and community organizations have officially endorsed the campaign , and many of them have been involved in the campaign itself. It has expanded the structures of collaboration between DSA’s rank-and-file and our elected officials, who have supported the campaign by hosting joint canvasses and appearing in campaign videos (more to come…). It has helped hundreds of ordinary people—including myself—develop concrete skills to lead the fight against capitalism and imperialism. When we began this campaign, we had a handful of dedicated organizers with one ambitious but deeply-felt goal. An arms embargo in New York City felt distant—just shy of impossible—but vitally necessary. A year later, we have hundreds of people involved in the campaign across several areas of work: creating communications, conducting research, speaking to workers in the field, hosting events, and more. We have plenty of work left to do, but an arms embargo, led by working people in solidarity with Palestine, feels closer than it ever has before. What is class struggle but this: the identification and exploitation of contradictions in the material system of capitalism; the politicization of working-class life as it already exists and the construction of new forms of collective power; the recognition of our shared destiny as peoples of this world and of our shared enemy in the class which destroys the conditions of life for its own enrichment? There are, of course, other forms of class struggle. Our task is the size of the world, the shape of the whole human project. To achieve it will require a diversity of tactics and struggle on many fronts. But to those for whom the arguments and ideas in this essay have rung true, to those who seek new avenues of action in solidarity with the people of Palestine, I invite you to join us in the fight for an arms embargo. If you are in New York City, you can fill out this form to get in contact with an onboarder for the Break the Chain campaign. Comrades in other chapters can reach out to DSA’s national Arms Embargo Organizing Committee to get connected to ongoing campaigns in your area or discuss how you might start one. articles.title: 25 Years Later: Afghan New Yorker Masuda Sultan Remembers 9/11 & 19 Relatives Killed in U.S. Bombing
articles.content: Almost 25 years ago, just days after the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center, President George W. Bush addressed the nation, making the case for war against al-Qaeda, whose leader, Osama bin Laden, was based in Afghanistan. “I sensed that something like this was not going to go unpunished,” Afghan American New Yorker and women’s rights activist Masuda Sultan told Democracy Now! at the time. Within a few weeks, the U.S. invasion began. Sultan would lose 19 members of her family when the U.S. military bombed their village outside of Kandahar. We revisit our coverage of the initial U.S. invasion, including our first interviews with Sultan in 2002, and speak to Sultan again today. She reflects on her experience, including working with Rita Lasar, the sister of a 9/11 victim, to advocate for acknowledgment and compensation for the families of Afghan civilians killed by the U.S. military. The United States war in Afghanistan lasted for nearly 20 years, the longest-ever active conflict in U.S. history. Now as the Taliban government — overthrown by the U.S. in 2001 and later reestablished following the end of U.S. military occupation in 2021 — tightens its patriarchal restrictions on women in Afghanistan, Sultan warns international actors not to “repeat the [mistakes of the] 1990s, of turning our backs on the country. We need to engage with the Afghan people, support Afghan women and support civil society.” Page 2 In the five years since the Taliban regained control of Afghanistan following the complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the country, millions of Afghan refugees have been forced out of neighboring Iran and Pakistan, where they had been living and “dumped at the border” without immediate access to food, water or shelter. At the same time, conditions for women and girls in Afghanistan continue to deteriorate, as basic rights to education, freedom of movement and access to services are increasingly curtailed under the Taliban’s authoritarian rule. “It’s a crisis for humanity,” says Jan Egeland, secretary general of the Norwegian Refugee Council, speaking to Democracy Now! from Kabul. “We’re so overstretched and underfunded. … We’re too alone on the ground here in Afghanistan,” explains Egeland, one of the few international aid workers continuing to support displaced people in the country. “The reason we have to lay off female aid workers, female teachers, teaching primary school girls, is because of lack of funding. It’s not because of the Taliban.” Despite the outsized role it played in destabilizing the country, there has been “zero funding” this year from the U.S. to humanitarian organizations operating in Afghanistan. “Don’t forget your promises when you went for the door abruptly five years ago,” Egeland says, addressing the United States and other, largely European, countries that made up the U.S.-led NATO coalition in Afghanistan.

articles.title: In defense of abolition
articles.author: Tempest National Committee
articles.content: Years ago I recognized my kinship with all living beings, and I made up my mind that I was not one bit better than the meanest on earth. I said then, and I say now, that while there is a lower class, I am in it, and while there is a criminal element I am of it, and while there is a soul in prison, I am not free. –Eugene V. Debs S ix years ago, the racist police murder of George Floyd sparked the biggest uprising in the history of the United States. Across the country, over 26 million people poured into the streets for months in a mass multiracial movement against the police and jails that enforce U.S. capitalism’s class and social inequalities. Calls to defund and abolish the police emerged as organic demands of the movement. The burning down of a Minneapolis police precinct proved more popular than both presidential candidates. Faced with a profound crisis of legitimacy, the two capitalist parties each in their own way launched a counteroffensive to shore up and expand the police state at the core of our bourgeois democracy. Tragically, some on the Left have adapted to the backlash. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently ridiculed the movement and its demands, quipping “ woke 1.0 was crazyyyyy ,” while Jacobin writers such as Paul Heideman, Eric Blanc, Ben Burgis, and Dustin Guastella have come out against defund and abolition in the name of what they describe as “mass politics.” Their position is not only profoundly mistaken, but dangerous. Their echoing of ruling-class attacks on abolitionism and support for the police surrenders the ideological ground won by the 2020 rebellion, undermines the struggle against President Trump’s authoritarianism, and impedes the fight for socialism. Ruling Class Backlash Their arguments must be understood in the context of the bipartisan backlash against Black Lives Matter. Each party has played its traditional role. In 2020, President Trump and his Republican Party assassinated the character of George Floyd, demonized BLM activists as terrorists, defended the police, rallied support for racist counterdemonstrations, turned vigilante Kyle Rittenhouse into a right-wing hero , and even threatened to deploy troops to repress protests. The Democrats, of course, pretended to be the movement’s ally, with lifetime supporters of policing like Nancy Pelosi donning kente cloth and bending her knee in the Capitol building. Mayors painted Black Lives Matter on city streets and enacted corporate Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) measures. They did so to co-opt the struggle and turn Black Lives Matter into Black Votes Matter for Joe Biden. The ruling class demobilized the movement, opening the door for both parties to increase funding for cops, ICE, CBP, and the FBI. From Compassionate Policing to Authoritarianism Once in power, President Biden vowed to “ fund, fund, fund the police .” He escalated the bipartisan war on migrants –shutting down the border, continuing the construction of Trump’s border wall, and ramping up deportations. Biden and Democratic governors and mayors proposed and, in many cases, passed bills named after George Floyd. These dramatically increased funding for policing and prisons under cover of fake reforms like community policing, body cameras, and professional training. Under Trump and Biden, national police expenditure increased by forty percent. The Democrats thereby re-legitimized and enacted the right’s law-and-order agenda. This has led to an increase in police murders every year since 2020 and paved the way for the return of the racist-in-chief Donald Trump and his white supremacist Republican Party. Despite the national drop in crime , Trump seized the opening provided by the Democrats, whipping up a racist moral panic over false claims about lawlessness, lies about Black criminality, nonsensical allegations of “reverse racism” against DEI, and a xenophobic assault on immigrants. Trump has funded, expanded, and weaponized the police state to an unprecedented degree. His “Big Beautiful Bill” poured $75 billion into the coffers of ICE to abduct immigrants and throw them into concentration camps. He deployed the National Guard to patrol Washington, D.C. in search of nonexistent criminals, reducing them to weeding the city’s unkempt gardens. He deployed his ICE Gestapo in city after city as an occupying army, resulting in the murders of Renee Good, Alex Pretti, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, Silverio Villegas González, and Isaias Sanchez Barboza, to name only a few. Many more have died in ICE concentration camps. When the killing of Good and Pretti triggered a city-wide uprising and a national day of protest, Trump unleashed his beefed-up surveillance state to snoop on activists in the name of controlling left-wing terrorism. His McCarthyite campaign led to charges against the Minneapolis 15 and the conviction of the Prairieland 9 . Now, with his popularity plummeting and his party certain to lose the midterms, Trump has taken aim at democracy itself in an attempt to rig the elections. He has gerrymandered districts, his Supreme Court has gutted the Voting Rights Act, and some like Steve Bannon are calling for ICE to be deployed at the polls to deter Black and Brown voters. Democratic Party Backlash and Left Accommodation The Democratic Party’s “resistance” to Trump’s ethnonationalist authoritarianism has been weak, counter-productive, and barely worthy of the name. This explains why the party’s approval rating remains essentially tied with that of the Republican Party at 40 percent. At best, the Democrats have demanded fake reforms to ICE, like body cameras and more training, which Trump happily enacted to legitimate his escalating war on migrants. Internally, the Democratic Party pressured its candidates to disavow any radical critiques of the police. Rather than stand up against this calumny, reformist politicians have disowned their previous positions. Their position is not only profoundly mistaken, but dangerous. Their echoing of ruling-class attacks on abolitionism and support for the police surrenders the ideological ground won by the 2020 rebellion, undermines the struggle against President Trump’s authoritarianism, and impedes the fight for socialism. Zohran Mamdani apologized for calling the police racist during his campaign for mayor of New York City. AOC dismissed the movement and the radicalization it produced as collective insanity. Mamdani defended her, saying people can change their positions, while he himself praised Jessica Tisch, his police commissioner, the law-and-order heir to a billionaire family, for lowering New York City’s crime rate. These reversals derive from their strategy of prioritizing electoral campaigns within a capitalist party over mass struggle. They wager that by abandoning their previous positions they can win elected office and advance socialist demands. In fact, they are capitulating to a capitalist party well-versed in co-opting and neutralizing the Left. Reformist Intellectuals Against Black Lives Matter Several self-avowed Marxists have supported AOC and Mamdani’s abandonment of abolitionism. Eric Blanc dismisses Black Lives Matter’s call for defunding the police and refunding systems of care as ultra-left and an impediment to their idea of “mass politics.” There are two key problems with this argument. First, as decades of Gallup polling have documented, the demand to shift funding from cops to care is actually popular . As some have pointed out , Jacobin ’s own polling data demonstrates that defund is more popular among working-class people than spending on mass transit. And second, even if defund wasn’t popular, raising the demand is both morally and strategically right. Remember, every major reform we’ve won from the abolition of slavery to suffrage, union recognition, civil rights, an end to the war in Vietnam, abortion rights, and gay marriage were initially unpopular. But a determined minority fought for them, won majority support, and used our collective power to protest and strike to force our rulers to concede them. But Blanc rejects that approach and instead argues for a strategy of reformism in the vain hope of using the capitalist state to enact socialism through legislation. As a result, he argues that politicians must downplay supposedly unpopular demands of oppressed people like defund in order to win “working class votes.” This class reductionism will backfire. It will shatter working-class unity by selling out oppressed people, lead reformist politicians to adapt to capitalist positions like law and order, lower rather than raise class consciousness and combativity, and thereby set back the very class and social struggles necessary to win reforms on the road to socialist revolution. That said, the debate about abolitionism is deeper than demands and strategy; it is about the goal. Paul Heideman makes that abundantly clear when he argues against defund and abolition, advocates that socialists adopt “carceral minimalism,” and cites as justification an article by Adaner Usmani and Chris Lewis that calls for hiring 500,000 more cops to control crime. These reformists believe, despite the mountain of evidence to the contrary, that the state and its police force can be wielded for social good in the present and to achieve socialism in the future. Advocating this position in the midst of the biggest expansion of authoritarian policing in U.S. history and its weaponization against unions, social movements, and the Left is bizarre, counterfactual, and unconscionable. They are empowering the ruling class to bolster a police state it will use to repress us all. Marxism is Abolitionism All these arguments are at odds with Marx and socialism from below, which is abolitionist to its core. Marx advocated the overthrow of the capitalist state, the establishment of workers’ democracy, and “the withering away of the state” itself. As Lenin argued, the socialist’s “ideal should not be the trade union secretary, but the tribune of the people, who is able to react to every manifestation of tyranny and oppression” to “ produce a single picture of police violence and capitalist exploitation” to advance the cause of socialism. Thus, Marxism is abolitionist . The goal of social revolution and abolition shapes our immediate practice. Faced with Trump’s deployment of the government police state, we should be demanding massive cuts to police, ICE, CBP, and the military and redistribution of that money to social programs that provide homes, jobs, education, and healthcare. In these struggles, socialists must reject the argument that police solve social harm. They don’t and never will. As the enforcers of class and social inequality, they are one of the main causes of social harm, as their skyrocketing record of brutality and murder demonstrates. Instead, we must combat the carceral state and all its ruling-class violence, racism, and dehumanization. We should therefore reaffirm our dedication to Marx’s abolitionist call at the end of the Communist Manifesto. “The Communists disdain to conceal their views and aims. They openly declare that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. Let the ruling classes tremble at a Communistic revolution. The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.” Opinions expressed in signed articles do not necessarily represent the views of the editors or the Tempest Collective. articles.title: Kenya’s crackdown on foreign traders raises fears of xenophobia and strains East African solidarity
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Fear and uncertainty spread among foreign traders in Kenya after President William Ruto directed authorities to move against small businesses operated by foreign nationals. The move triggered a scramble among some immigrant communities to seek protection, regularize their status, or leave the country. The directive, announced earlier this month, has particularly unsettled Burundian traders, many of whom operate small informal businesses in Nairobi and other urban centers. Hundreds of Burundians sought assistance and travel documentation from their embassy in Nairobi in fear that the government’s new policy could lead to deportations or further harassment. The government has since moved to soften the impact of the initial announcement by providing a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals to regularize their status, following pressure from Kenyans who said it could lead to xenophobia. But the clarification was perhaps too late, as isolated incidents of violence and looting involving businesses operated by Burundians were already registered, including reports of traders having goods taken or destroyed occurred. For lawyer Waringa Wahome, the issue is not just about immigration compliance or competition between traders. She argues that the language used by political leaders can have direct consequences for vulnerable communities. “What are the risks of presidential rhetoric targeting foreign traders particularly Burundians, Rwandans, and other East Africans, and could such statements contribute to xenophobia, ethnic profiling, harassment or violations of migrants’ rights?” Wahome asked. “The rhetoric creates a target on their backs” Wahome, an advocate of the High Court and community legal advocate, told BreakThrough News , that the consequences were already visible in Nairobi’s informal settlements. She pointed to incidents reported in Mathare, where foreign traders were allegedly attacked and their goods taken or destroyed. “In Mathare, the morning of 8 September smelled of the horrific incidents of the night,” Wahome said. “On one hand, a hardworking Rwandese had all his chapati and flour for his chapati business violently taken away. For others it was an opportunity to loot from the Ugandan and Rwandese run businesses.” “The rhetoric against the traders creates permanently a target on their backs exposing them to risk and violating their freedoms,” she said. Wahome argued that the situation should be understood against the wider vulnerability of Kenya’s working class. Describing the conflict as “horizontal violence” between economically insecure Kenyans and equally vulnerable migrant workers, warning that ethnic profiling and discrimination could deepen existing social divisions. “This horizontal violence among this section of an unsecure working class of Mathare was sparked by a sweeping presidential rhetoric calling on the crackdown, mass expulsion and criminalization of the foreign traders specifically running small businesses,” Wahome said. She also questioned whether targeting small traders addresses the underlying causes of Kenya’s economic difficulties. “The majority of the Kenyan youth is poor, unemployed and hopeless,” she said, pointing to rising living costs, widening inequality, shrinking civic space, and concerns over corruption and public resources. “In that context,” Wahome says “a sweeping rhetoric such as that made by President Ruto can only be seen as a statement meant to deflect attention from the structural economic plunder.” What does the law protect? The legal questions are significant. Kenya has the power to regulate immigration, employment, and business activity by foreign nationals. The government says its current exercise is designed precisely to establish who is legally entitled to work or conduct business in the country and to give those who are not compliant an opportunity to regularize their status. But Wahome argues that enforcement cannot become collective punishment. “The law protects a human being first for being a human being and therefore they have inviolable rights including the right to dignity and to be treated with dignity,” she said. Kenya ratified the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights in 1992. Article 2(6) of the Kenyan Constitution provides that treaties and conventions ratified by Kenya form part of Kenyan law. Wahome points specifically to the African Charter’s protections of human dignity and its restrictions on the expulsion of non-nationals. Even where a migrant’s documentation is irregular, enforcement should be individualized and lawful. “States are obligated to ensure that all migrant workers and members of their families in an irregular situation have non-discriminatory and effective access to such regularization procedures and that the procedures are not applied in an arbitrary manner,” Wahome said. She added that the 90-day window must not simply become a countdown to mass enforcement. “Every case must be treated on its own in a fair process which respects the fundamental rights of the migrant workers.” A test for East African integration The controversy has also exposed a difficult contradiction within East Africa’s regional integration project. Kenya, Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda are members of the East African Community, whose Common Market framework provides for the free movement of people, workers, services and capital, as well as rights of establishment and residence. The EAC says its Common Market is based on principles including non-discrimination on grounds of nationality and equal treatment of nationals of other Partner States. The right to establish a business, however, is not an unlimited license to ignore national laws. The EAC itself states that citizens have the right to establish businesses in another Partner State in accordance with the national laws of that state. Kenya can enforce its immigration and licensing laws. The question is whether it can do so without turning the enforcement exercise into a campaign against an entire nationality or category of African migrants. Wahome sees the danger as extending beyond individual traders. “The small-scale traders represent the majority of the youth population of Africa,” she said, describing them as university and technical-school graduates who have been unable to find formal employment or obtain capital to establish businesses. “They are the children of the working class of Kenya, East Africa and Africa,” she added. Further describing the reported violence as “manufactured violence targeted at the poor,” arguing that the businesses at the center of the dispute, selling tea, mandazi and other basic goods have little capacity to determine the structural direction of Kenya’s economy. “The President is creating a false enemy and fracturing pan-African solidarity,” Wahome said, arguing that poor Kenyans were being encouraged to view small East African traders as the reason for unemployment and the rising cost of living. The political movement Kongamano la Mapinduzi, issued a statement too, “Kongamano la Mapinduzi strongly condemns William Ruto’s recent remarks that essentially ordered a crackdown on foreigners running small businesses in Kenya,” the statement said. “We at Kongamano la Mapinduzi wish to make it clear that an African head of state should be uniting Africans, not turning African people against one another.” The movement framed the dispute within the longer Pan-African project of removing barriers between African peoples. “While our shared Pan-African struggle has always envisioned a united Africa without borders, Ruto’s remarks have today set Kenya along the dangerous path of criminalization and harassment of African traders in the name of protecting local businesses,” the statement said.
